tour.title: New Creation in John: From "In the Beginning" to the Garden Tomb
tour.intro: You asked what John means by "new creation" and how the Genesis allusions work. The short answer, as you'll hear: John doesn't just quote Genesis — he rebuilds his whole Gospel on its skeleton, from the opening line through a seven-day first week, a wedding, a garden, and a breathing that redoes Genesis 2:7. This tour walks you through that architecture so you can start seeing it yourself.

steps.why: Tim and Jon set the frame: in Genesis 1 the light doesn't eliminate the darkness, it contains it — "the seventh day has no evening," the day the light wins. John capitalizes on that momentum: the darkness trying to overcome the light at the cross, and the resurrection as the moment "darkness is not able to overcome the light anymore." This is the cleanest definition of new creation as new life in Jesus set against the "anti-creation or the decreation forces of darkness."

Why can we be sure John is deliberately echoing Genesis? Because "in the beginning" is "blindingly obvious," and behind it sits Proverbs 8's Lady Wisdom, itself "a reading of Genesis 1" — God's word and ruach as the means of creation. This shows John composing his opening as a retelling of Genesis, with light and word doing the creating, and it explains the phrase "God's word is the light shining in the darkness."
steps.episodeTitle: Why Are There Four Accounts of the Gospel?

steps.why: From the opening page the hosts read Jesus as the new Adam: humans were given the image and dominion of God to spread light and order, "but we fail that creation mandate... and start spreading darkness and chaos instead of order." Jesus remakes and reclaims it all as "the new Adam, as the new human" — and the hosts make the crucial John point that "God heals creation whenever he becomes part of it," which they call John's soteriology, his theory of salvation.
steps.episodeTitle: John 1: In the Beginning Was the Word

steps.why: Here's the Genesis skeleton made explicit: count the days in John 1–2 and you get seven — day one "in the beginning," then successive "next day" markers, landing on Cana's "on the third day," so "four days plus three would be day seven... and the end of seven days, we get a wedding." Seven is the number of completeness, and John "is often setting up seven so that we are looking for the eighth to find new creation." It's a map for reading the whole Gospel.
steps.episodeTitle: Gospel of John Overview: A Unique Eyewitness

steps.why: Now the wedding sign itself. The hosts track the water imagery through John: wells are where patriarchs meet their wives, so "water episode is marriage episode," and the six stone jars "set aside and empty" for purification get refilled — "he's getting ready to do a new cleaning." They hear the wilderness rock struck for water behind it, and wine that points to the wedding banquet and the messianic reign. New creation begins with purification and a wedding.

A caution against flattening the allusions. NT Wright reads the water jars as pointing to "the ultimate purification which Jesus will offer" on the cross, but insists this is "not the cancellation of the Judean way of life" — John's Gospel "is a way of tracking through the great stories in Israel's scriptures and saying, now at last we see where it was all going." He ties it to Jesus as the true temple, "the place where heaven and earth meet... earth is shot through with the life of heaven."
steps.episodeTitle: Why did Jesus turn water into wine? Did Paul invent Christianity? Are Christian hymns wrong? NT Wright Explains

steps.why: The Genesis allusions come home in a garden. The commentary walks Mary's morning: weeping at the tomb, she "turned around and the morning sun is bright in her eyes... thinking he was the gardener," until Jesus says her name — "Mary" — and she answers "Rabboni." In John, the first day of the week begins in a garden with the one who tends it calling his own by name, the echo of Eden's gardener.

The tour ends where John's new creation becomes personal: Jesus breathes on the disciples and says "Receive the Holy Spirit," and the teacher spells out that this "recalls what God did... in Genesis chapter 2, verse 7, when God formed Adam out of the dust of the ground and then breathed on him." He calls it recapitulating: "here it is, the humanity restored, here it is, life reborn." Same breath as the first creation, now making new humans.

tour.closing: So here's what you can take away: for John, new creation isn't a slogan — it's a story being told again. The same Word who spoke light into the darkness in Genesis speaks again in flesh; a week of seven days leads to a wedding and then to an eighth day; the water of purification becomes the wine of the feast; and the risen Jesus is found in a garden, breathing life into his people the way God breathed into the dust. Every Genesis echo is John saying the same thing: the first creation has found its true human, and what began in a garden is being remade from an empty tomb.
